kurals.tamil:
தொடங்கற்க எவ்வினையும் எள்ளற்க முற்றும்
இடங்கண்ட பின்அல் லது.
kurals.transliteration:
Thodangarka evvinaiyum ellarka mutrum
Idanganda pinnal lathu.
kurals.meaning: Begin no action against an enemy, and do not look down on him, until you have found ground from which you can surround and overcome him.
kurals.elementary: Before a game of hide-and-seek, a smart player first looks around for the best hiding spot, and never thinks the seeker is too silly to find them. Valluvar says to do the same with any big task: find the right spot first, and never think the other side is weak.
kurals.university: The chapter opens the third member of the triad that runs through chapters 48 to 50: strength (vali), time (kaalam) and now place (idam). The key word is ‘mutrum idam’, a place from which one can encircle or besiege (mutruthal, to surround, to lay siege); Parimelazhagar and the modern word-glosses (for example thirukkural-thamizh.org) take it as the ground suited for investing the enemy. The two prohibitions are joined: ‘thodangarka’ (do not begin) and ‘ellarka’ (do not despise), so over-confidence and bad positioning are treated as a single error. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah take ‘ellarka’ as ‘do not scorn the enemy’, whereas Kalaignar reads it as ‘do not treat the undertaking itself as trivial’, a minor interpretive variant. Older printed texts give the sandhi form ‘தொடங்கற்க வெவ்வினையு மெள்ளற்க’, which modern editions split as ‘எவ்வினையும் எள்ளற்க’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya opens Book IX of the Arthashastra by telling the would-be conqueror to weigh his own and his enemy’s power, place and time before marching, and he defines a good place as ground suited to the manoeuvres of one’s own army and unsuited to the enemy’s.
hinduism.explanation: For Kautilya, desha (place) is one of the things a king has to calculate before starting any campaign, together with strength and the right season.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar gives the same order: work out the ground first, and only then begin.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book IX, Chapter 1 (tr. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel (power, place, time) with the three-chapter sequence in the Kural; paraphrased, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock… And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts two builders: one picked solid ground and his house stood, the other picked sand and his house fell.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the outcome is decided by choosing the right ground before starting to build.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong image of choosing ground before acting, but Jesus uses it as a metaphor for obeying his teaching, not for strategy.

islam.quote_or_event: Before Badr, the Companion al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir asked the Prophet whether the chosen campsite was fixed by revelation or was a matter of war and strategy. When told it was strategy, he advised moving forward to the wells nearest the enemy, and the Prophet accepted.
islam.explanation: The early biography presents this as a model of choosing a position carefully before fighting begins, by taking control of the water.
islam.tie_back: It fits the Kural’s rule not to begin until the right position has been found.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad), account of Badr
islam._accuracy_note: Close thematic match; this is a sira report, paraphrased, and not Quran or sahih hadith.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Do not despise any man, and do not discriminate against anything, for there is no man that has not his hour, and there is no thing that has not its place.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Azzai warns that nobody should be dismissed, because every person has a moment and every thing has its place.
judaism.tie_back: The mishnah brings together the Kural’s two concerns, not despising the other side (ellarka) and taking place seriously.
judaism._accuracy_note: Both ‘do not despise’ and ‘its place’ appear, but the mishnah is about humility, not military positioning.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha describes Himalayan ground where only monkeys can go and level ground where hunters lay tar traps. Wise monkeys see the trap and keep away, while a careless monkey walks onto the hunter’s ground and gets stuck in five places.
buddhism.explanation: He uses the story to warn monks against leaving their proper range (their own territory) for someone else’s ground.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the fatal mistake is acting before judging whether the ground belongs to you or to your enemy.
buddhism.source: Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.7, Makkata Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Clear ‘own ground and enemy’s ground’ logic, but the sutta is about mental discipline, not war.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As Xerxes advanced in 480 BCE, the Greek allies debated where to make their stand, first at Tempe and then at the narrow pass of Thermopylae with the strait of Artemisium beside it, and they chose the pass because the narrows would cancel out Persian numbers.
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus shows the Greeks picking the position before committing to battle, having judged that the terrain mattered more than headcount.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s advice in practice: settle the ground first, then begin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Historical narrative rather than myth; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you know the enemy and know yourself, your victory will not stand in doubt; if you know Heaven and know Earth, you may make your victory complete.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu ends his chapter on terrain by saying that knowing the ground (Earth) is what makes victory complete.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts treat knowing the ground as something you need before acting, and neither lets you underestimate the enemy.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War X.31 (tr. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close; from the ‘Terrain’ chapter itself.

kurals.tamil:
முரண்சேர்ந்த மொய்ம்பி னவர்க்கும் அரண்சேர்ந்தாம்
ஆக்கம் பலவுந் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Muranserntha moimbi navarkkum aransernthaam
Aakkam palavun tharum.
kurals.meaning: Even for people who are already strong in war, fighting from a secure, fortified position brings many extra advantages.
kurals.elementary: Even the strongest kid in a snowball fight does better behind a snow wall. Being strong is good, but being strong and in a safe spot is much better.
kurals.university: ‘Muran’ means hostility or opposition and ‘moimbu’ means strength, so the first line describes people strong enough to take on an enemy. ‘Aran’ is the fortress, one of the six limbs of the state that later gets its own chapter (74, அரண்), and ‘aakkam’ is gain or prosperity. The ‘-um’ (even) in ‘navarkkum’ is the point: position adds to strength and is no substitute for the lack of it, which is why Parimelazhagar reads the verse as saying that even the mighty gain from a secure base. Modern glosses widen ‘aran’ to any safe place of operation, not only a walled fort (thirukkural-thamizh.org: ‘the place of action is safe’). Older printings show the sandhi ‘மொய்ம்பி னவர்க்கு மரண்சேர்ந்தா மாக்கம்’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As enemies do not hurt these (beings, when they are) sheltered by (their) fortresses, even so foes (can) not injure a king who has taken refuge in his fort.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu lists the kinds of forts (desert, water, forest, earthwork, armed camp, hill) and compares a king in his fort to animals that are safe in their own shelters.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, this makes the aran (fortified position) a source of power beyond the king’s own strength.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Direct parallel on the value of a fortified position; Manu is prescriptive where the Kural is observational.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says the community he is founding will stand on a rock that no hostile power can overcome.
christianity.tie_back: The image is a secure foundation that makes its occupants hard to overcome, which is the Kural’s aran.
christianity._accuracy_note: Only an image-level parallel; the verse is ecclesiological and not about tactics.

islam.quote_or_event: At the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq, 627 CE), the outnumbered Muslims of Medina dug a trench across the open northern approach on Salman al-Farisi’s advice, and the confederate army could not force its way through.
islam.explanation: A prepared defensive line let a much smaller force hold off a large coalition until the siege fell apart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural says a secure position adds advantages even to fighters who are already strong, and the trench did this for Medina.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (tr. A. Guillaume), account of the Trench; cf. Quran 33:9–25
islam._accuracy_note: Close historical parallel; the trench comes from sira tradition, while the Quran refers to the siege without describing the trench.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs counts the rock-hyrax among creatures that are small but very wise, because it makes up for weakness by living among rocks.
judaism.tie_back: The hyrax is a picture of the Kural’s aran: safety comes from where you are.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good fit, though the proverb stresses the weak finding safety, while this kural speaks of the strong gaining more.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares a disciple to a king’s frontier fortress with a deep foundation post, a moat, a patrol road, many weapons, troops, a wise gatekeeper, high walls and ample stores. Such a fortress cannot be taken by enemies from outside.
buddhism.explanation: Each part of the fortress stands for a spiritual quality that keeps the practitioner safe from Mara.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s point that a fortified position multiplies security is the literal basis of this simile.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.63 (7.67 in some editions), Nagara Sutta: The Fortress
buddhism._accuracy_note: The fortress-as-security logic is the same, but the application is spiritual; paraphrased.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Athens asked Delphi about the Persian invasion, the oracle said that a ‘wooden wall’ alone would stay unconquered. Themistocles took this to mean the fleet and persuaded the Athenians to place their hope in the ships and the waters around Salamis.
greek_mythology.explanation: Athens survived by picking the defensive position that suited it best, which was the sea, rather than trusting its city walls.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural says the right place of refuge multiplies a people’s strength, and the Athenians found theirs in the ships.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong thematic parallel; the oracle’s wording is paraphrased here.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The good fighters of old first put themselves beyond the possibility of defeat, and then waited for an opportunity of defeating the enemy.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu says securing yourself comes before attacking, and is something within your own control.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s secured base (aran) is exactly this first step of making yourself impossible to defeat.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War IV.1 (tr. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in logic; Sun Tzu speaks of disposition generally rather than fortified places specifically.

kurals.tamil:
ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி அடுப இடனறிந்து
போற்றார்கண் போற்றிச் செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aatraarum aatri adupa idanarinthu
Potraarkan potrich cheyin.
kurals.meaning: Even the weak become strong enough to defeat their enemies if they choose the right place and keep themselves protected while acting against the foe.
kurals.elementary: A little cat on a high shelf can bat at a big dog that can’t reach it. The cat isn’t stronger, it just picked the right spot. Valluvar says even weak people can win if they choose their spot well and stay safe.
kurals.university: The verse turns on the wordplay ‘aatraarum aatri’: those who lack power (aatraar) come to have it (aatri) and destroy the enemy (adupa). ‘Potraar’ literally means ‘those who do not honour us’, a standard Kural word for enemies, and the next word ‘potri’ (having guarded, taken care) repeats the sound with the opposite meaning. Parimelazhagar reads ‘potri’ as the actor protecting himself, so the conditions for success are knowing the place and staying self-protected. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah follow this reading; Kalaignar adds the idea of choosing the right place for the attack. The kural spells out what 492 implied: the right place can make up for missing strength, and not merely add to strength one already has.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the meditator to set up a firm seat in a clean place, neither too high nor too low, and only then to begin controlling the mind.
hinduism.explanation: Even inner discipline starts with choosing and securing the right spot, because an unsteady position works against the practitioner.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘idan arinthu… potri’ (know the place, guard yourself, then act) matches the yogi’s order of preparation.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Weak match: the same principle of preparing the place first, but in a contemplative setting with no adversary.

christianity.quote_or_event: “After these things Jesus walked in Galilee: for he would not walk in Jewry, because the Jews sought to kill him.”
christianity.explanation: John says Jesus deliberately worked in Galilee and stayed away from Judea while his opponents there were looking for a chance to kill him.
christianity.tie_back: He kept his mission going by choosing a safer place of action, much like the Kural’s ‘potraarkan potri’ (guarding oneself among enemies).
christianity._accuracy_note: Real parallel in choosing where to act for safety, but there is no idea of defeating an enemy here.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Remember] when you were on the near side of the valley, and they were on the farther side, and the caravan was lower [in position] than you.”
islam.explanation: The Quran recalls where each side stood at Badr, when a small and poorly equipped Muslim force defeated a much larger Quraysh army.
islam.tie_back: The verse points to positioning at a battle where the weaker side won, which is the Kural’s claim.
islam._accuracy_note: The verse notes the positions but credits the outcome to divine decree, not to tactical choice.

judaism.quote_or_event: At Michmash, Jonathan and his armour-bearer climbed a narrow crag between two rocky outcrops and attacked a Philistine outpost from a position where the enemy could not bring its numbers to bear. Their success set off a wider Philistine rout.
judaism.explanation: Two men beat a garrison by using a narrow, high approach the enemy did not expect.
judaism.tie_back: The weak defeating the strong by knowing the ground is the Kural’s ‘aatraarum aatri adupa’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good fit; the narrative also credits divine help and the Philistines’ panic.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If only I had kept to my proper range today, to my own ancestral territory, this hawk would have been no match for me in battle.”
buddhism.explanation: A quail caught by a hawk talks its way free, returns to a ploughed field full of clods, dodges behind one, and the diving hawk breaks its own breast on it.
buddhism.tie_back: The weak bird beats the strong one only because it fights from ground it knows, which is exactly what this kural says.
buddhism.source: Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.6, Sakunagghi Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one parallel; the sutta then applies it to the monk’s mental ‘range’.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before Salamis, Themistocles argued that fighting in the narrow strait favoured the smaller Greek fleet, while open sea favoured the larger Persian one, and the Greeks won by fighting in the narrows.
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus records the argument and the victory that followed, which saved Greece.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The weaker side won by picking where to fight, as the Kural says.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A Kid standing on the roof of a house, out of harm’s way, saw a Wolf passing by and immediately began to taunt and revile him. The Wolf… said, ‘Sirrah! I hear thee: yet it is not thou who mockest me, but the roof on which thou art standing.’”
philosophy.explanation: The fable ends with the moral that time and place often give the weak an advantage over the strong.
philosophy.tie_back: That moral restates Kural 493, together with the previous chapter’s point about time.
philosophy.source: Aesop, The Kid and the Wolf (tr. G. F. Townsend)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Moral almost identical to the kural; the fable is folk wisdom rather than systematic philosophy.

kurals.tamil:
எண்ணியார் எண்ணம் இழப்பர் இடனறிந்து
துன்னியார் துன்னிச் செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Enniyaar ennam izhappar idanarinthu
Thunniyaar thunnich cheyin.
kurals.meaning: If those who have found the right place stay close to it and act from it, enemies who planned to beat them will have to drop their plans.
kurals.elementary: A turtle pulled all the way into its shell makes the curious dog give up and walk away. When you are in the right place and stay there, the other side stops trying.
kurals.university: The verse repeats words in pairs: ‘enniyaar ennam’ (the plan of those who planned) and ‘thunniyaar thunni’ (those who reached the place, keeping close to it). ‘Thunnuthal’ means to approach, cling to or stay close; commentators read the second ‘thunni’ as keeping firmly to the chosen ground instead of drifting away from it. Parimelazhagar takes ‘enniyaar’ as enemies who expected to win, and ‘ennam izhappar’ as more than tactical defeat: they give up the intention itself. Kalaignar has the foe not even daring to think of victory, and Pulavar Kesikan takes ‘thunni’ as pressing the battle closely. Where 493 was about winning, this kural is about deterrence: the right position ends the contest before it begins.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Sabha Parva, Krishna tells Yudhishthira that the Yadavas, worn down by Jarasandha’s repeated invasions of Mathura, moved to Kushasthali (Dvaraka), a fortress on the sea. There they felt safe from his attacks.
hinduism.explanation: Instead of fighting on exposed ground, the Yadavas took a position their powerful enemy could not easily reach.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural says, taking and holding the right place frustrates an enemy who planned to win.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Sabhā Parva, Section 14 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good fit; the details of the move differ across the Mahabharata and Harivamsa, and it is paraphrased here.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus sends his disciples into hostile territory and tells them to be shrewd about how they move there.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s idea of knowing where you stand so that enemies’ designs fail is close to the ‘wise as serpents’ half of this saying.
christianity._accuracy_note: General call to prudence among enemies; nothing specific about position.

islam.quote_or_event: “And Allāh repelled those who disbelieved, in their rage, not having obtained any good.”
islam.explanation: This verse closes the Quran’s account of the Trench, when the confederate army besieging Medina gave up and left empty-handed.
islam.tie_back: Enemies who ‘planned’ to take Medina ‘lost their plan’ (ennam izhappar) once the defenders held their prepared ground.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the outcome closely; the Quran credits God’s wind and hosts, while the trench comes from sira tradition.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the children of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites that inhabited Jerusalem; but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Benjamin in Jerusalem unto this day.”
judaism.explanation: The Jebusites held their hill-city so firmly that the tribe of Benjamin had to give up trying to expel them.
judaism.tie_back: A people fixed in a strong place outlasted their attackers’ plans, which is Kural 494’s scenario.
judaism._accuracy_note: The outcome fits, but the verse gives no reason and later tradition frames it as Israel’s failure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Realizing that this body is as fragile as a clay pot, and fortifying this mind like a well-fortified city, fight out Mara with the sword of wisdom. Then, guarding the conquest, remain unattached.”
buddhism.explanation: The verse tells the practitioner to make the mind a fortified city from which Mara, the tempter, can be fought off.
buddhism.tie_back: Holding a fortified position so that the attacker’s design fails is the kural’s point, moved inward.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Only a metaphorical parallel; the ‘enemy’ is inner defilement.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Behind the walls of Troy, the Trojans held off the Achaean army for ten years. The besiegers never took the city by assault, and in the end had to resort to the trick of the wooden horse.
greek_mythology.explanation: A strong position frustrated a superior coalition for a decade, until the defenders were drawn out of their own security.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As long as the Trojans stayed with their ground (thunni), the attackers’ plans kept failing, which is the Kural’s point.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad (siege narrative), and Odyssey 8.492–520 on the horse
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good illustration, but it is epic myth and the city does eventually fall.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Hence the skillful fighter puts himself into a position which makes defeat impossible, and does not miss the moment for defeating the enemy.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu says a well-chosen position removes the enemy’s chance of winning.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim that holding the right place makes the enemy’s plans come to nothing.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War IV.14 (tr. Lionel Giles)

kurals.tamil:
நெடும்புனலுள் வெல்லும் முதலை அடும்புனலின்
நீங்கின் அதனைப் பிற.
kurals.transliteration:
Nedumpunalul vellum muthalai adumpunalin
Neengin athanaip pira.
kurals.meaning: In deep water the crocodile overpowers other creatures, but once it leaves the water, those same creatures overpower it.
kurals.elementary: A fish is the best swimmer in the pond, but put it on the grass and it can hardly move. The crocodile is the same: a champion in the river, in trouble on dry land.
kurals.university: This is the chapter’s best-known image. ‘Nedumpunal’ is deep or wide water; ‘adum’ (kills, overcomes) is placed in the middle so that it can be read with either half. Parimelazhagar’s construction is: in deep water the crocodile defeats others; if it leaves the water, others (pira) kill it. The verse leaves out the verb of the second clause and borrows it from ‘adum’, typical Kural compression. The Sanskrit nīti tradition has the same image in a Pañcatantra verse (nakraḥ svasthānam āsādya gajendram api karṣati), where the crocodile in its own place drags even a lordly elephant but out of it is beaten by a dog. That suggests a shared South Asian stock of proverbs rather than direct borrowing.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “nakraḥ svasthānam āsādya gajendram api karṣati | sa eva pracyutaḥ sthānāc chunāpi paribhūyate”
hinduism.explanation: In its own place, the crocodile drags even a king of elephants; the same crocodile, fallen from its place, is overpowered even by a dog.
hinduism.tie_back: This Sanskrit maxim is almost a twin of Kural 495, crocodile included.
hinduism.source: Pañcatantra III (Kākolūkīya), v. 43/46 depending on edition; cited in Apte and Böhtlingk–Roth s.v. nakra (wisdomlib.org)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one parallel; the Sanskrit is verified, and the English gloss here is our own.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm says the righteous person does well like a tree planted in its proper place beside water.
christianity.tie_back: It gives the positive side of the crocodile image: in its right element, a living thing is at full strength.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that strength depends on the right element, but has no contrast of loss outside it.

islam.quote_or_event: At Uhud the Prophet told his fifty archers, “Stick to your place, and don’t leave it even if you see birds snatching us, till I send for you.” When most of them left the hill to collect booty, the Quraysh cavalry circled round, and the Muslims were routed.
islam.explanation: The archers were decisive on their hill and became helpless once they left it.
islam.tie_back: Like the crocodile leaving the water, a force that abandons its own place gives its strength away.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close; the hadith also stresses obedience to the commander.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If we are afraid in the water, our natural habitat which gives us life, then in a habitat that causes our death, all the more so.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Akiva tells of a fox inviting frightened fish onto dry land, and the fish refuse because leaving their element would kill them for certain. He applies the parable to Israel and Torah.
judaism.tie_back: The same creature-out-of-its-element logic as the crocodile verse.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 61b (William Davidson/Koren translation, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Striking parallel in image; Akiva’s application is spiritual and national.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As a fish when pulled out of water and cast on land throbs and quivers, even so is this mind agitated.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares the untrained mind to a fish thrown onto land, helpless and thrashing.
buddhism.tie_back: The water creature that loses its power on land is the Kural’s central image.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Same image; applied to the mind rather than to strategy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The giant Antaeus, son of Earth, could not be beaten while he touched the ground, which kept renewing his strength. Heracles defeated him by lifting him off the earth and crushing him in the air.
greek_mythology.explanation: Antaeus’s strength belonged to his element; taken out of it, he was easily beaten.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the Greek crocodile, invincible in his own place and powerless once removed from it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I well deserve my fate, for what business had I on the land, when by my nature and habits I am only adapted for the sea?”
philosophy.explanation: A crab that leaves the shore to feed in a meadow is eaten by a fox and blames itself as it dies.
philosophy.tie_back: Almost the crocodile kural in fable form: a sea creature is lost on land.
philosophy.source: Aesop, The Crab and the Fox, Perry 116 (tr. G. F. Townsend)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close; Townsend’s moral is about contentment rather than strategy.

kurals.tamil:
கடலோடா கால்வல் நெடுந்தேர் கடலோடும்
நாவாயும் ஓடா நிலத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Kadalodaa kaalval nedunther kadalodum
Naavaayum odaa nilaththu.
kurals.meaning: A tall chariot with strong wheels cannot run on the sea, and a ship that sails the sea cannot run on land.
kurals.elementary: A bicycle is great on the road but useless in a swimming pool, and a boat is great in the pool but useless on the road. Every tool, and every person, has a place where it works best.
kurals.university: The kural uses a paired image: ‘kaal val nedunther’, the tall chariot with strong wheels (kaal, literally ‘leg’, here the wheel), and ‘naavaay’, the sea-going ship, a word related to Sanskrit nau and Latin navis, which shows early Tamil familiarity with maritime trade. The repeated verb ‘odaa’ (will not run) connects the two lines. Parimelazhagar reads the verse as an allegory for forces: land armies and naval forces each succeed only in their own element, so a king must match his forces to the terrain. Kalaignar makes it a general lesson that whoever chooses where to act must at least know that a chariot will not cross the sea. The thirukkural-thamizh.org gloss extends it to countries bordered by mountains, forests, sea or desert, each needing its own methods.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya describes different kinds of battlefield and matches each arm of the army to suitable ground: chariots need level, firm, open terrain, elephants can handle uneven and marshy ground, and infantry can fight almost anywhere.
hinduism.explanation: Classical Indian military science treats choosing terrain for each arm as an exact skill.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s chariot-and-ship image is the poetic form of this technical rule.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book X, Chapter 4 (tr. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close technical parallel; paraphrased from the chapter on battlefields.

christianity.quote_or_event: “They ran the ship aground; and the forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable, but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the waves.”
christianity.explanation: In Paul’s shipwreck off Malta, the ship that had carried them across the sea was stuck and broken once it hit land.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ship that ‘does not run on land’, told as an actual event.
christianity._accuracy_note: A concrete instance of the image; Luke tells it as narrative, not as a lesson about place.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs are the ships in the sea, like mountains. If He willed, He could still the wind, and they would remain motionless on its surface.”
islam.explanation: The Quran points to great ships as signs of God, whose power depends on the conditions of the sea and wind.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats the ship’s strength as dependent on its proper element.
islam._accuracy_note: Only an image-level parallel; the verse is about divine signs, not choosing a place.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And took off their chariot wheels, that they drave them heavily: so that the Egyptians said, Let us flee from the face of Israel.”
judaism.explanation: Pharaoh’s chariots, the best weapon of their time on dry land, got stuck in the seabed and lost their wheels.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s chariot that ‘does not run on the sea’ appears literally in the Exodus story.
judaism._accuracy_note: Vivid parallel in image; the Torah credits God’s intervention rather than bad terrain choice.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the raft simile, the Buddha describes a man who builds a raft to cross a flood and then carries it on his head over dry land. He asks whether that is the right use of a raft, and the monks agree it is not.
buddhism.explanation: A tool built for water becomes a burden on land; the Dhamma is to be used for crossing over, not clung to.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ship that cannot run on land makes the same point: something useful in one element is useless in another.
buddhism._accuracy_note: The image matches; the Buddha’s lesson concerns non-attachment, not strategy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Pylos (425 BCE), Thucydides notes the strange reversal of the Athenians, a sea power, defending from land, while the Spartans, a land power, attacked from ships and tried in vain to force a landing on a rocky shore.
greek_mythology.explanation: Each side was fighting outside the element it was strong in, and the Spartan assault failed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the chariot-at-sea and ship-on-land problem in real Greek history.
greek_mythology.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 4.11–14 (tr. Richard Crawley)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong parallel; history rather than myth, paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Moor your craft higher up than the enemy, and facing the sun. Do not move up-stream to meet the enemy. So much for river warfare.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu gives separate rules for mountains, rivers, salt-marshes and flat country, because each kind of ground needs its own tactics.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it holds that methods suited to one terrain fail in another.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War IX.6 (tr. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Terrain-specific tactics fit the kural’s logic, but the chosen line is narrow.

kurals.tamil:
அஞ்சாமை அல்லால் துணைவேண்டா எஞ்சாமை
எண்ணி இடத்தால் செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Anjaamai allaal thunaivendaa enjaamai
Enni idaththaal seyin.
kurals.meaning: If you think everything through without leaving anything out and act from the right place, you need no other ally except fearlessness.
kurals.elementary: If you have practised your speech, checked every page, and are standing in the right spot on stage, the only thing left to bring is courage. This kural says good planning and the right place leave you needing only a brave heart.
kurals.university: ‘Enjaamai enni’ means to think things through without remainder (enjuthal, to be left over), so planning comes first. ‘Idaththaal seyin’ means acting from, or by means of, the right place; the instrumental ‘-aal’ makes place the means of action. ‘Anjaamai allaal thunai vendaa’ says no ally is needed except fearlessness, so courage takes the place of all outside help. Parimelazhagar notes that thorough deliberation and the right ground remove the need for allies (thunai), which were discussed earlier under ‘Valiyarithal’ (ch. 48, thunaivali). Kalaignar’s gloss is about thorough method and leaves out place, a lighter reading than the traditional one.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna lists abhayam, fearlessness, first among the divine qualities (daivī sampad) that lead to freedom.
hinduism.explanation: In the Gita, fearlessness heads the list of virtues belonging to a person of divine nature.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise makes fearlessness the one companion needed once planning and positioning are done.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the priority on fearlessness; the Gita’s context is spiritual qualities rather than tactics.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand. Stand therefore…”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to prepare fully, then hold their ground firmly.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Having done all, to stand’ matches the Kural’s thorough preparation followed by steadfast courage in position.
christianity._accuracy_note: Preparation-then-stand is close; Paul’s ‘armour’ is spiritual and God is the ally.

islam.quote_or_event: “Those to whom people said, ‘Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them.’ But it [merely] increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Sufficient for us is Allāh, and [He is] the best Disposer of affairs.’”
islam.explanation: After Uhud, believers who were warned of a gathering enemy answered with fearlessness instead of alarm.
islam.tie_back: The refusal to be frightened by numbers matches the Kural’s ‘no ally but fearlessness’.
islam._accuracy_note: The fearlessness fits, but the Quran names God as the sufficient ally, which the Kural does not.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.”
judaism.explanation: God charges Joshua to be courageous as he leads Israel into the land and its campaigns.
judaism.tie_back: Courage as the leader’s essential quality going into the field fits the Kural’s ‘anjaamai’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on courage; the ally here is God, and the Kural’s stress on planning and place is missing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no fear for an awakened one, whose mind is not sodden (by lust) nor afflicted (by hate), and who has gone beyond both merit and demerit.”
buddhism.explanation: For the Dhammapada, a well-trained mind no longer knows fear.
buddhism.tie_back: The kural’s fearlessness as one’s only needed companion has an inner counterpart here.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Parallel on fearlessness only; nothing about planning or place.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Thermopylae, when the Spartan Dieneces was told the Persian arrows were so many they would hide the sun, he answered that this was good news, because they would then fight in the shade.
greek_mythology.explanation: Herodotus records the reply as an example of fearlessness in a well-chosen position against huge odds.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Once the ground was chosen, fearlessness was the only thing the Greeks still needed, as the Kural says.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close combination of good ground and fearlessness; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The natural formation of the country is the soldier’s best ally; but a power of estimating the adversary, of controlling the forces of victory, and of shrewdly calculating difficulties, dangers and distances, constitutes the test of a great general.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu calls terrain an ally in itself, provided the general calculates everything carefully.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts treat the right ground plus full calculation as removing the need for other allies.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War X.21 (tr. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong parallel on ‘ground as ally’ and thorough calculation; Sun Tzu does not single out courage here.

kurals.tamil:
சிறுபடையான் செல்லிடம் சேரின் உறுபடையான்
ஊக்கம் அழிந்து விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sirupadaiyaan sellidam serin urupadaiyaan
Ookkam azhinthu vidum.
kurals.meaning: If a commander with a small army stands on ground where his strength counts, the commander of a large army will lose his drive and his advantage.
kurals.elementary: In a narrow hallway, one kid can block the way even if ten kids are trying to get through, because only one can squeeze in at a time. A small team in the right spot can stop a big team.
kurals.university: ‘Sellidam’ is the key word: ‘the place where one’s power prevails’ (sellu, to be current or valid, as with a coin that ‘passes’). Parimelazhagar reads it as ground favourable to the small army, where it can fight on its own terms. ‘Urupadaiyaan’ is the commander of a large or mighty army, and ‘ookkam’, his drive and self-confidence (the subject of chapter 60), is what gets destroyed. Solomon Pappaiah gives a different reading: when the large army goes after the small one into the place where the small one lies, the large army’s prestige is lost. The sense stays the same, but the grammar of ‘sellidam’ is read in another way.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One bowman, placed on a rampart, is a match in battle for one hundred (foes), one hundred for ten thousand; hence it is prescribed (in the Sastras that a king will posses) a fortress.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu puts a number on the advantage of position: a single archer on a wall equals a hundred attackers.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the small force on its own ground overcoming the large one, as the Kural describes.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close; Manu speaks of forts in particular, the Kural of favourable ground in general.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews recalls heroes such as Gideon, Barak and David who, weak in numbers, routed much larger forces.
christianity.tie_back: It celebrates the few defeating the many, the outcome this kural describes.
christianity._accuracy_note: The outcome matches, but Hebrews credits faith rather than position.

islam.quote_or_event: “How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allāh. And Allāh is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: Before facing Goliath’s army, the faithful few under Saul (Talut) remind themselves that small forces have often beaten large ones.
islam.tie_back: The Kural gives the practical means, favourable ground, by which a small force can win.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear small-over-large parallel; the Quran credits divine permission and patience.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The children of Israel pitched before them like two little flocks of kids; but the Syrians filled the country.”
judaism.explanation: The Arameans thought Israel’s God ruled only the hills and chose to fight on the plain, yet the small Israelite force still won.
judaism.tie_back: The passage is openly about choosing terrain against a small army, though it overturns the Aramean assumption.
judaism._accuracy_note: Terrain is central, but the Bible denies that terrain decides the outcome, which reverses the Kural’s premise.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Tacchasūkara Jātaka, wild boars terrorised by a tiger are organised by a clever boar (the Bodhisatta). They dig pits and take up positions on prepared ground, so that when the tiger leaps, it falls into a pit and is killed.
buddhism.explanation: Weak animals defeat a far stronger predator by preparing the ground where the fight happens.
buddhism.tie_back: The small force on its own prepared ground breaks the strong one’s spirit, which is the kural’s scenario.
buddhism.source: Jātaka No. 492, Tacchasūkara Jātaka (ed. E. B. Cowell)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Thematically apt; details summarised from memory of the Cowell translation, so medium confidence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Thermopylae, a few thousand Greeks led by Leonidas and his 300 Spartans held the narrow pass for days against Xerxes’ huge army. Repeated Persian assaults, including the elite Immortals, failed until a traitor showed the Persians a mountain path around the pass.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the narrows, Persian numbers counted for nothing, and the Great King’s confidence was badly shaken.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the classic case of ‘sirupadaiyaan sellidam’, the small army on its own ground ruining the large army’s drive.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “With a superior force, make for easy ground; with an inferior one, make for difficult ground.”
philosophy.explanation: Wu Tzu, quoted by Chang Yu in Giles’s notes, advises the smaller army to seek broken terrain where numbers cannot be deployed.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s rule for the small army put as a maxim.
philosophy.source: Wu Tzu, quoted in Chang Yu’s commentary on Sun Tzu III.17 (Giles, The Art of War, 1910)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near-exact parallel; found in Giles’s annotated edition, not in Sun Tzu’s main text.

kurals.tamil:
சிறைநலனும் சீரும் இலரெனினும் மாந்தர்
உறைநிலத்தோடு ஒட்டல் அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Sirainalanum seerum ilareninum maanthar
Urainilaththodu ottal arithu.
kurals.meaning: Even people who have no strong fort and no special strength are hard to beat when you attack them in the land where they live.
kurals.elementary: Even a small puppy barks bravely and is hard to chase out of its own house, because it knows every corner. People are hardest to beat at home.
kurals.university: ‘Sirai nalan’ is the excellence of an enclosure or defensive barrier (sirai also means a moat or a prison-wall), and ‘seer’ is any other kind of distinction or strength. ‘Urainilam’ is the land where people live, their home ground, and ‘ottal’ is read by Parimelazhagar as going there to engage them. The kural balances 492: there the advantage came from fortification, here it comes from simply being at home, with the home fighter’s knowledge of the land and motivation. The thirukkural-thamizh.org gloss makes the psychology explicit: the knowledge that one is defending one’s own place is itself a source of courage. The verse also works as a warning to the invader, who is always at a disadvantage on foreign ground.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In weighing campaigns, Kautilya advises the conqueror to consider whether the ground suits his own forces or the enemy’s. He treats the enemy’s home terrain, where the defender knows the land and the invader does not, as a factor that raises the cost of attack.
hinduism.explanation: Classical Indian statecraft counts the defender’s familiarity with his own land among the things to be calculated.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural states the resulting rule plainly: people are hard to beat in their own land.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book IX, Chapter 1 (tr. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Only a general parallel; Kautilya has no line stating this kural’s point directly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “When a strong man armed keepeth his palace, his goods are in peace.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of a householder guarding his own house, who can be overcome only by someone stronger.
christianity.tie_back: The defender in his own dwelling is secure, which fits the Kural’s ‘urainilam’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Apt image, but the next verse shows the stronger one prevailing, and the context is spiritual conflict.

islam.quote_or_event: “When Allah’s Messenger (ﷺ) besieged Taif and could not conquer its people, he said, ‘We will return (to Medina) If Allah wills.’”
islam.explanation: After the victory at Hunayn, the Muslim army besieged Taif but could not take it and withdrew.
islam.tie_back: It illustrates how hard it is to dislodge people from their own home ground.
islam._accuracy_note: The outcome fits, but Taif had strong walls, whereas the kural speaks of people without forts.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The river of Kishon swept them away, that ancient river, the river Kishon. O my soul, thou hast trodden down strength.”
judaism.explanation: Deborah’s song celebrates Israelite tribes defending their own hill-country, where the invader Sisera’s nine hundred iron chariots were swept away by the local river.
judaism.tie_back: Lightly armed people on their own land beat a far better-equipped invader.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good ‘home ground’ fit; the song credits heaven and the river as fighting for Israel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Suṃsumāra Jātaka, a crocodile tricks a monkey onto its back to steal its heart. The monkey says its heart hangs on the fig tree, gets carried back to the bank, leaps into the tree and cannot be caught.
buddhism.explanation: Once the monkey is back in its own tree, the crocodile has no power over it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s people at home, the monkey is safe in its own place.
buddhism.source: Jātaka No. 208, Suṃsumāra Jātaka (ed. E. B. Cowell)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Apt folk parallel; the story also turns on wit, not only on position.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Darius invaded Scythia, the Scythians, who had no towns or farmland to defend, kept retreating across their own steppe and refused pitched battle. Their king Idanthyrsus told Darius they had nothing he could force them to defend, and the Persian army eventually had to withdraw.
greek_mythology.explanation: A people without forts or fixed wealth proved impossible to conquer in their own land.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s case: no ‘sirai nalan’, and still ‘ottal arithu’, hard to attack at home.
greek_mythology.source: Herodotus, Histories 4.120–142, esp. 4.127 (tr. A. D. Godley)

philosophy.quote_or_event: Clausewitz argues that the defensive form of war is in itself stronger than the offensive, because the defender benefits from terrain, local support and waiting, while the attacker grows weaker the further he advances into hostile country.
philosophy.explanation: His analysis explains why invading someone’s homeland is so costly.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the theory behind the Kural’s observation that people are hard to beat on their own ground.
philosophy.source: Carl von Clausewitz, On War, Book VI, Chapter 1 (tr. J. J. Graham)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual parallel; paraphrased rather than quoted.

kurals.tamil:
காலாழ் களரில் நரியடும் கண்ணஞ்சா
வேலாள் முகத்த களிறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaalaazh kalaril nariyadum kannanjaa
Velaal mukaththa kaliru.
kurals.meaning: A fearless war elephant that has impaled spear-carrying soldiers on its tusks can be killed even by jackals once it is stuck in mud where its feet sink.
kurals.elementary: A huge elephant is the strongest animal in the forest, but if it gets stuck in deep mud, even small animals can bother it and it can’t fight back. Being big and strong doesn’t help if you’re stuck in the wrong place.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with its strongest contrast. ‘Kaal aazh kalar’ is mire or saline swamp where legs sink; ‘kann anjaa’ is ‘unflinching of eye’, never afraid; ‘velaal mukaththa kaliru’ is the tusker that carries spear-bearing warriors (velaal) impaled on its tusks (mukam, the front), which Parimelazhagar explains as an elephant that has gored armed soldiers. The ‘nari’ is the jackal, the most contemptible of predators, so the verse sets the mightiest animal against the meanest. The old continuous text (thirukkural-thamizh.org) shows the sandhi ‘காலாழ் களரி னரியடுங் கண்ணஞ்சா வேலாண் முகத்த களிறு’, where ‘வேலாண்’ is ‘வேலாள்’ joined to ‘முகத்த’. The kural returns to 491’s warning: the greatest strength, put on the wrong ground, falls to the weakest enemy.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Karna Parva, the left wheel of Karna’s chariot sinks into the earth in the middle of his duel with Arjuna. While Karna struggles to lift it free, the peerless warrior is struck down.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata’s great tragic hero is not beaten by lack of skill or courage but by ground that gives way under him.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the fearless war elephant stuck in the mire, told of a human champion.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Karṇa Parva, Sections 90–91 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel; the epic also points to curses and fate behind the sinking wheel.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist thanks God for lifting him out of sinking mud and putting his feet on firm ground.
christianity.tie_back: The contrast between miry clay and a rock underfoot is the Kural’s contrast between the swamp and firm footing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close image of sinking ground against firm ground; the psalm is about deliverance, not strategy.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Remember] when He… sent down upon you from the sky, rain by which to purify you… and to make steadfast your hearts and plant firmly thereby your feet.”
islam.explanation: Before Badr, rain firmed up the sandy ground under the Muslim position. Commentators add that the same rain made the Quraysh side heavy and slippery.
islam.tie_back: Firm footing for one side and bad ground for the other is exactly the kural’s lesson.
islam._accuracy_note: ‘Plant firmly your feet’ fits well; the effect on the enemy’s ground comes from tafsir, not the verse itself.

judaism.quote_or_event: Sisera, commander of nine hundred iron chariots, the elite weapon of his day, lost the battle by the river Kishon when the ground turned against his chariots. He fled on foot and was killed by Jael, a tent-dwelling woman.
judaism.explanation: The most feared force in Canaan was destroyed by bad ground and finished off by an unlikely hand.
judaism.tie_back: This is the mighty tusker in the mire, killed by the weakest of foes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel; the narrative credits God and Jael’s courage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Delight in heedfulness! Guard well your thoughts! Draw yourself out of this bog of evil, even as an elephant draws himself out of the mud.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada uses the familiar image of an elephant stuck in a bog to urge vigilance.
buddhism.tie_back: Same image as the kural, the mighty elephant helpless in mud, turned into advice to get out of it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Identical image; the application is moral rather than military.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad 21, Achilles, unmatched on the plain, fights the river-god Scamander in his own element. The flood breaks down on him, the ground washes away beneath his feet, and the greatest warrior of Troy nearly drowns until the gods step in.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even Achilles is almost undone once he fights in the river’s domain rather than on firm ground.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the tusker in the mire, the mightiest fighter becomes helpless where his footing gives way.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Vivid parallel; paraphrased, and Achilles is saved rather than killed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In crossing salt-marshes, your sole concern should be to get over them quickly, without any delay.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu treats marshland as dangerous ground where an army must not linger or give battle if it can avoid it.
philosophy.tie_back: His warning rests on the Kural’s point that boggy ground can destroy even a mighty force.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War IX.7 (tr. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Direct advice about marsh terrain; no contrast of mighty against weak.
